clue.text: Go for somewhere in Scotland, as Dickens character

parts.note: to go for something is to choose or pick it
Wick is a town in Caithness in the far north of Scotland

explanation.surface: A traveller picks a Scottish destination while dressing up as a Dickens character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as' is only a link. Mr Pickwick heads The Pickwick Papers.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Pickwick is the genial founder of the club in Dickens's first novel, The Pickwick Papers.

clue.text: Dickens character in a jumble, say?

indicators.note: say signals that the word for a jumble is to be heard, not spelt

parts.note: a jumble or untidy pile is a heap

explanation.surface: A muddled Dickens character, perhaps found among a pile of others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a' is link padding; the pile word HEAP sounds like the name Heep.
explanation.definitionFit: Uriah Heep is the fawning, 'umble' clerk who schemes against everyone in David Copperfield.

clue.text: Appear clumsy as Dickens character

definitions.meaning: to move or act in an awkward, blundering way
The pompous parish beadle in Oliver Twist

explanation.surface: Someone plays a bungling Dickens figure and looks awkward doing it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as' links the two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means stumble about ineptly, and Bumble is the beadle who runs the workhouse in Oliver Twist.

clue.text: Dead clever eating meal that's topped and tailed

indicators.note: eating means the word for clever takes the trimmed meal word inside it

parts.note: deft means skilful or clever

indicators.note: topped and tailed means the meal word loses its first and last letters

parts.note: lunch is a midday meal

explanation.surface: A dead-clever diner eats a meal with the ends trimmed off, like vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dead clever' reads as slang for very clever, but 'Dead' alone is the definition; 'eating' and 'that's topped and tailed' are the two indicators.
explanation.definitionFit: Defunct means no longer living or operating, so it is a synonym for dead.

clue.text: Homer's issue about cleaner illustration of comparative values

indicators.note: about means the son's name goes around the cleaner word

parts.note: Bart is the son of Homer Simpson in The Simpsons
a char or charlady is an old British word for a cleaning woman

explanation.surface: Homer's problem with a cleaner is shown on a graph of comparative values.
explanation.walkthrough: 'issue' looks like a problem but means offspring. A char is a British cleaning lady.
explanation.definitionFit: A bar chart compares quantities using bars of different lengths, a graphic display of relative values.

clue.text: Unlikely rich setter will be giving more

indicators.note: unlikely suggests the letters of rich setter are arranged in an improbable new order

explanation.surface: A rich setter is unlikely to be generous with money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'will be' is a link. The surface is about money, but the definition is about elasticity.
explanation.definitionFit: Something stretchier has more give, yielding further when pulled, as fabric or elastic does.

clue.text: Devout prayer not quite about English breakfast food

indicators.note: about means the shortened believer word goes around the abbreviation for English
not quite means the last letter of the believer word is left off

parts.note: a devout person praying five times daily might be a Muslim

explanation.surface: A pious worshipper says a short prayer before an English breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not quite' trims MUSLIM to MUSLI, and 'about' wraps it around E.
explanation.definitionFit: Muesli is a cereal mix of oats, nuts and dried fruit eaten in the morning.

clue.text: Nice to be flexible in steady job that's cushy

indicators.note: in means the rearranged letters sit within the word for steady

parts.note: sure means steady or firm, as in sure-footed

indicators.note: flexible means the letters of Nice can bend into another order

explanation.surface: A pleasant steady post where flexibility makes it comfortable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nice' looks like praise of the job, but it is the fodder; 'to be flexible' rearranges it and 'in' places it.
explanation.definitionFit: A sinecure is a paid position needing little or no work, the definition of an easy berth.

clue.text: Monarch — a king for a day

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for king, from the Latin rex
Thur is a short form of Thursday

explanation.surface: A king who reigns for just one day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur is the legendary king of Camelot, and also several real British kings' names in waiting.

clue.text: Bound to be captain

definitions.meaning: to bound is to leap or hop lightly along
the captain of a curling or bowls team

explanation.surface: Someone is destined to lead the team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound to be' reads as destined, but 'Bound' is a leap; 'to be' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Skip means jump lightly, and in bowls and curling the team leader is called the skip.

clue.text: Vulgar, a notable stinker

parts.note: blue means smutty or vulgar, as in blue jokes
a cheese, as in big cheese, is an important person

explanation.surface: A rude remark about some famous rotter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a' is a link. A big cheese is a notable person, and a blue joke is a crude one.
explanation.definitionFit: Veined cheeses such as Stilton and Roquefort are famously pungent, so they are notorious smelly foods.

clue.text: Infusion — put it back together

indicators.note: back means the word it is read in the other direction

parts.note: someone together is composed and sane

explanation.surface: An instruction to reassemble an infusion that has been taken apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put' is a link; 'back' turns IT into TI. 'Together' means level-headed, not assembled.
explanation.definitionFit: A tisane is a herbal tea made by steeping leaves or flowers in hot water.

clue.text: Oh dear, wars destroyed those honed for battle

indicators.note: destroyed signals the letters of the phrase are broken up and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A lament that wars have destroyed soldiers trained for combat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'those honed for battle' suggests trained troops, but honed means sharpened.
explanation.definitionFit: Arrowheads are the sharpened tips of arrows, ground keen for use in war.

clue.text: Shout to fielder about right for Dickens character

indicators.note: about means the cry to the fielder goes around the abbreviation for right

parts.note: a cricket fielder under a high ball hears the call 'catch it!'

explanation.surface: A cricketer yells at a fielder, which suits a Dickens character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' is a link. The call is the one shouted when a cricket ball goes up in the air.
explanation.definitionFit: Bob Cratchit is Scrooge's underpaid clerk in A Christmas Carol, father of Tiny Tim.

clue.text: Stars drinking alcohol — slippery slopes!

indicators.note: drinking means the word for stars takes the drink inside it

parts.note: suns are stars, the Sun being one
kir is a drink of white wine with blackcurrant liqueur

explanation.surface: Celebrities drinking heavily are on a slippery slope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slippery slopes' sounds like moral decline, but the slopes are snowy pistes.
explanation.definitionFit: Ski runs are snow-covered tracks down a mountain, slick and steep enough for skiing.

clue.text: Fools accepting price for salts

indicators.note: accepting means the fools word takes the price word inside it

parts.note: nits, short for nitwits, are fools
a rate is a price or charge

explanation.surface: Fools accept a price for some salts.
explanation.walkthrough: Salts here are chemical compounds, not table seasoning.
explanation.definitionFit: Nitrates are salts of nitric acid, widely used as fertilisers.

clue.text: Trotter, extremely restricted by Dickens character, won't work

indicators.note: restricted by means the ends of Trotter are confined inside the Dickens name

parts.note: Bill Sikes is the brutal burglar in Oliver Twist

indicators.note: extremely points to the outermost letters of the word Trotter

explanation.surface: A trotting horse is penned in by a Dickens villain and refuses to work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trotter' is a horse or pig's foot but only gives its ends TR.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who strikes withdraws labour in protest, refusing to do their job.

clue.text: Deliver criminal, arresting old villain

indicators.note: arresting means the rearranged letters hold the abbreviation for old inside
criminal suggests the letters of Deliver are bent into a crooked order

explanation.surface: Delivering a criminal by arresting an old villain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'criminal' makes EVILDER from DELIVER, and 'arresting' takes O into it.
explanation.definitionFit: An evildoer is a wrongdoer or wicked person, a synonym for a villain.

clue.text: Insects under teacup

indicators.note: under in a down answer means the insects come below the tea word

parts.note: cha, or char, is British slang for tea
lice are small parasitic insects

explanation.surface: Insects found crawling beneath a teacup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'teacup' looks like one word but splits into tea and cup.
explanation.definitionFit: A chalice is a goblet or ornate drinking cup, especially one used for Communion wine.

clue.text: Dickens character taking issue with dragon

parts.note: an issue of a magazine is a mag
a dragon is a fierce old woman, likewise called a witch

explanation.surface: A Dickens character takes issue with a fierce dragon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking' and 'with' are links. 'taking issue' looks like disagreeing.
explanation.definitionFit: Abel Magwitch is the escaped convict who becomes Pip's secret benefactor in Great Expectations.

clue.text: A seesaw covering middle of big bird cage

indicators.note: covering means the word for seesaw wraps around the central letter

parts.note: to seesaw is to fluctuate, or vary

indicators.note: middle of points to the central letter of the word big

explanation.surface: A playground seesaw sits over the middle of a big birdcage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seesaw' looks like a noun but is the verb fluctuate.
explanation.definitionFit: An aviary is a large enclosure for keeping birds, a walk-in cage.

clue.text: Dickens character going back and forth

indicators.note: going back and forth says the name reads identically in both directions

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: A Dickens character pacing to and fro.
explanation.walkthrough: The surname of Pip, hero of Great Expectations, reads the same both ways.
explanation.definitionFit: Philip Pirrip, known as Pip, is the narrator of Great Expectations.

clue.text: Appropriate Dickens character

definitions.meaning: here a verb: to take for oneself, often dishonestly
Herbert ... is Pip's friend and roommate in Great Expectations

explanation.surface: A suitable Dickens character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appropriate' looks like the adjective suitable, but it is the verb meaning seize.
explanation.definitionFit: To pocket something is to take it for yourself, and Herbert Pocket befriends Pip.

clue.text: Lithium injected into lamb etc I cooked with steel and tin, perhaps?

indicators.note: injected into means the element symbol goes inside the reworked letters
cooked suggests the letters of lamb etc I are stewed into a new order

parts.note: Li is the chemical symbol for lithium

explanation.surface: A cook injects lithium into lamb and other things, using steel and tin pans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cooked' gives BIMETAC, and 'injected into' places the lithium symbol. The question mark marks steel and tin as just one example pair of metals.
explanation.definitionFit: Bimetallic means made of two metals, as a strip of steel bonded to another metal is.

clue.text: Large spruce

explanation.surface: A big spruce tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spruce' looks like the conifer, but here it is the adjective neat.
explanation.definitionFit: A tidy sum is a sizeable one, and tidy also means neat and orderly.

clue.text: Finally get a bit of wood

definitions.meaning: to grasp something at last, as in the penny dropped
a small thin stick from a tree branch

explanation.surface: Someone at last obtains a piece of timber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finally' looks like a last-letter signal but is part of the first definition: to cotton on at last.
explanation.definitionFit: To twig is British slang for understand suddenly, and a twig is a small woody shoot.

clue.text: Animosity in good Dickens character

parts.note: Barnaby Rudge is the title character of a Dickens novel

explanation.surface: Bad feeling found within a decent Dickens character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A grudge is lasting resentment or ill will towards someone.

clue.text: Verse minister cut and cut again

indicators.note: cut means the clergyman word has its last letter chopped off

parts.note: a cleric is a member of the clergy, a minister
to hew is to chop or cut, a second cut after the first

explanation.surface: A poem about a minister who was censored twice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut' trims CLERIC to CLERI; the second 'cut' is a synonym, HEW.
explanation.definitionFit: A clerihew is a comic four-line biographical poem, invented by Edmund Clerihew Bentley.
